newsitem.title: INDIA: Poll code blocks solution to India tax protest.
newsitem.headline: Poll code blocks solution to India tax protest.

text.p: Cinema-owners and commodities traders who have gone on strike to demand lower taxes in India's commercial capital of Bombay will get no respite until March because of poll regulations, officials said on Thursday.

A code of conduct that took effect ahead of a series of elections to local self-government bodies in Maharashtra state where Bombay is located, prevents the government from taking any steps to lower taxes, an election official told Reuters.
Cinema-owners have indefinitely downed shutters since January 1 to protest against a proposed steep hike in taxes which would double the cost of tickets for buyers.
They feared that such high prices would drive away patrons.
The tax hike was scheduled to take effect from January 1.
Bombay is the capital of India's movie industry, and where 106 of an estimated 1,300 cinemas in Maharashtra are located.

Traders in Bombay's sugar, cotton, oilseeds, bullion and metals markets held a one-day strike on Thursday to protest against higher sales-tax and stamp duty regulations that also went into effect on January 1.
But a senior election official said the state government would be unable to take any step to lower the taxes until early March, when the elections are scheduled to conclude.
"Any favours to be distributed during the election period would influence voters," said D.N. Chaudhary, the state's election commissioner.
"Any act of the ruling political party, when it extends a concession, gives it an advantageous position to attract voters," he added.
Chaudhary said, independent candidates and aspirants of other political parties would be unable to make similar concessions.
"The elections have to be free and fair," he said.
The elections, to village-level government bodies and city municipal corporations, are scheduled to run from the end of January until early March, election officials said.
Chaudhary said the code of conduct for the polls had "full legal force", though it was not strictly a law. Political parties infringing the code of conduct could be taken to court, he added.
